title: Count the cost first
hook: before you begin anything, look at what comes first and what follows, like an athlete before the games (Enchiridion 29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: who handed you over? Your line was my mind is mine. When someone's words started steering, did you take the keys back? Day three hundred sixty-one.
screen: `WHO HANDED YOU OVER? — MY MIND IS MINE.`

segments.voice: Every January, gyms fill up. New shoes, new water bottles, new plans. By February, a lot of those shoes are back in the closet. Nobody stopped wanting to be fit. What happened is that the plan was all beginning and no middle: nobody pictured the five-forty alarm in the dark, the sore knees, the Thursday they didn't feel like it. Epictetus saw the same thing in his students, two thousand years before gym memberships, and he used an athlete to show it. Today: count the cost first.
screen: `JANUARY: NEW SHOES.` → `FEBRUARY: BACK IN THE CLOSET.` → `ALL BEGINNING, NO MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In every undertaking, Epictetus says, look at what comes before it and what follows from it, and only then set about it. Otherwise you'll start eagerly, because you haven't thought about what comes next, and later, when some hard parts show up, you'll give up in shame. Second, the athlete. You want to win at Olympia? So do I, he says, it's a fine thing. But look at what comes first and what follows. You'll have to keep to a strict routine, eat on a schedule, stay off sweets, train at set hours in heat and cold, give up cold drinks and wine when you're told, hand yourself over to the trainer as to a doctor. Then in the contest you may dislocate a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a lot of dust, take a beating, and after all that, lose. Third, the children. If you don't count the cost, he says, you'll be like children who play wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpeters, then actors, trying everything and finishing nothing. Weigh it all, and then, if you still want it, go ahead. Fourth, a neighbor. The same picture appears in the Gospel of Luke, about following Jesus, in the King James words: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" A different teacher, a different calling, the same sitting down before you start. Epictetus' point isn't to scare anyone off. It's that people who have already seen the middle are better placed to get through it. Count it, and if you still want it, begin.
screen: `WHAT COMES FIRST, WHAT FOLLOWS.` · `THE ATHLETE: DIET, DUST, A BEATING.` · `LIKE CHILDREN TRYING EVERYTHING.` · `SIT DOWN FIRST, AND COUNT.` · then, large: `FIRST, WHAT FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Choose one plan you're about to start. A project, a habit, a trip, a hard conversation. Picture the beginning: it's easy to see. Now walk forward into the middle. What will the third week ask of you? What will you give up? Where will it get boring, or hard, or embarrassing? See it plainly, the way Epictetus lists the dust and the twisted ankle. Then, at the end, ask: do I still want it? Notice the answer. The bell holds the time.
Count the cost first. Epictetus' rule for every undertaking: look at what comes before and what follows, like an athlete before the games, then begin. Today's word.
Your line: first, what follows. Before you say yes to anything new today, take one minute to picture the middle. Day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners, before taking on something new, picture its demands and setbacks in detail and only then decide whether to begin.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 29: the Olympic games, at Olympia.

trapdoor: what you thought: think before you act.
what it means: picture the middle and the end of a plan, its costs and setbacks, then begin if you still want it.
what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 29 is nearly word for word Discourses 3.15, one of the clearest places where Arrian's handbook draws straight from the longer notes.
